apnea-ecg-database.name: Apnea-ECG Database

schema_org.description: 70 overnight single-lead ECG recordings from 30 subjects, contributed by Thomas Penzel of Philipps-University Marburg and released as the data for the PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2000. Each recording runs a full night — 6.75 h to 9.62 h, 573.7 hours in total — digitised at 100 Hz with 12-bit resolution at 200 A/D units per millivolt, from a single unnamed ECG channel. The reference annotation is per minute: an expert marked each of the 34,313 recorded minutes as apnea or not, on the basis of simultaneously recorded respiration and oxygen saturation, and 13,064 of them are apnea. Records also carry the apnea, hypopnea and apnea-hypopnea indices and the subject's age, sex, height and weight. The release divides itself into a 35-record learning set (a01-a20 apnea, b01-b05 borderline, c01-c10 control) and the 35 test records x01-x35 whose answers were withheld until the challenge closed and posted in 2020; that division is NOT subject-disjoint and ECGBench does not use it as a split. Eight records have companions carrying chest, abdominal and nasal respiration and SpO2, which are not part of this partition because their ECG is byte-identical to the plain record's.
schema_org.name: Apnea-ECG Database

bidmc-congestive-heart-failure-database.name: BIDMC Congestive Heart Failure Database

schema_org.description: 15 long-term two-lead ECG recordings of subjects with severe congestive heart failure, NYHA class III-IV — 11 men aged 22 to 71 and 4 women aged 54 to 63 — recorded at Boston's Beth Israel Hospital (now Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center) while receiving conventional medical therapy, prior to entering a trial of oral milrinone. Each record is roughly 20 hours of ambulatory Holter, 19.77 h to 20.00 h, digitised at 250 Hz with 12-bit resolution over a nominal +/-10 mV and band-limited to about 0.1-40 Hz; the two channels are named ECG1 and ECG2 in the headers with no statement of which anatomical leads they are. The shipped annotations are 1,622,282 beat labels produced by an automated detector and never manually corrected, of which 38,524 are ventricular and 5,314 supraventricular, plus 258 rhythm markers delimiting atrial fibrillation in 4 of the 15 records. There is no diagnostic label to predict: every subject is in the same severity class, which is what makes this the severe-CHF cohort against which a normal or mixed-arrhythmia database is compared.
schema_org.name: BIDMC Congestive Heart Failure Database

brno-university-of-technology-ecg-qualit.name: Brno University of Technology ECG Quality Database (BUT QDB)

schema_org.description: Eighteen single-lead electrocardiograms, each longer than 24 hours, recorded from 15 subjects (9 female, 6 male, aged 21 to 83) between August 2018 and October 2019 with a Bittium Faros 180 chest recorder while they went about ordinary daily life — "free-living conditions", the only restriction being no bathing or swimming. 478.7 hours of ECG at 1,000 Hz, with 3-axis accelerometry at 100 Hz alongside every recording. The point of the release is signal quality: three ECG experts graded the ECG sample by sample into three classes — all waveforms measurable, QRS detectable but nothing finer, and unusable — and the database ships each expert's opinion and their consensus. Three recordings are graded end to end and the other 15 in two 20-minute segments each, plus five further segments chosen for being noisy, giving 99.4 hours of sample-level ground truth. It is a quality-assessment benchmark, not a diagnostic one: there is no cardiac diagnosis anywhere in the release.
schema_org.name: Brno University of Technology ECG Quality Database (BUT QDB)

schema_org.description: 363 twelve-lead electrocardiograms, one per individual, from people investigated for Brugada syndrome at Hospital Universitario Central de Asturias, Oviedo, Spain. Each record is 12 seconds at 100 Hz. Brugada syndrome is characterised by coved-type ST-segment elevation in the right precordial leads V1-V3, often with a right bundle branch block pattern, and carries a risk of sudden cardiac death. Every subject carries three binary or ternary clinical labels: the Brugada diagnosis itself (healthy, confirmed, or other/atypical), whether the baseline ECG pattern is pathological, and whether the subject experienced sudden death.

cipa-ecg-validation-study.name: CiPA ECG Validation Study

creator.name: US FDA / CDER; Phase I Clinical Pharmacology Study (NCT03070470)

schema_org.description: 5,749 ten-second 12-lead ECGs at 1 kHz from 60 healthy volunteers in the CiPA Phase I ECG biomarker validation study (SCR-004, NCT03070470), a double-blind randomised trial testing whether QTc together with J-Tpeakc can separate balanced ion-channel block from predominant hERG block using Phase I data alone. Fifty subjects (1001-1050) were randomised in parallel to three days of ranolazine, verapamil, lopinavir+ritonavir, chloroquine or placebo, ten each; ten more (2001-2010) took part in a two-period crossover of dofetilide against diltiazem+dofetilide. Records were extracted in triplicate at 28 nominal timepoints spanning -1 to 73 hours from dosing, and each is published both as the raw 10 s segment and as a derived 16-channel median beat carrying semi-automatic P-onset, QRS-onset, QRS-offset, T-peak and T-offset annotations on the vector-magnitude lead. Per-record heart rate, RR, PR, QRS, QT, QTcF, J-Tpeak, J-Tpeakc and Tpeak-Tend accompany the waveforms, alongside plasma concentrations of each analyte and subject demographics. No participant had cardiac disease: the label of interest is drug exposure, not diagnosis.

code-15-pct-telehealth-network-of-minas-.name: CODE-15% (Telehealth Network of Minas Gerais, 15% subset)

schema_org.description: 345,779 twelve-lead ECGs from 233,770 patients, an openly licensed 15% sample of the CODE cohort gathered by the Telehealth Network of Minas Gerais (TNMG) from primary-care units across Brazil. Every recording is stored as 4,096 samples at 400 Hz — 10.24 s — with shorter acquisitions zero-padded symmetrically to that length. Six binary abnormality labels ship per record (1dAVb, RBBB, LBBB, SB, ST, AF), derived from the TNMG's own reports, plus a `normal_ecg` flag, age, sex, a neural-network age estimate, and mortality follow-up for the 233,647 records that have it. 37,775 records (10.9%) carry at least one of the six abnormalities and 3,671 carry more than one. Because 66,929 patients contributed more than one recording — up to 38 — folds are grouped on patient_id.

code-test-827-record-hold-out-test-set.name: CODE-test (827-record hold-out test set)

creator.name: Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais / TNMG

schema_org.description: 827 twelve-lead ECGs from 827 distinct patients of the CODE cohort, published as the hold-out test set of Ribeiro et al. 2020 and notable less for its size than for its annotation. Six binary abnormalities (1dAVb, RBBB, LBBB, SB, AF, ST) were labelled independently by two cardiologists, with a third senior specialist adjudicating every disagreement to produce the gold standard; four further sets of annotations — two 4th-year cardiology residents, two 3rd-year emergency residents, two 5th-year medical students, and the paper's own neural network — ship alongside it, which is what makes the release usable for studying reader agreement rather than only for scoring a classifier. Against the gold standard, 146 of the 827 records (17.7%) carry at least one abnormality and 12 carry more than one. Every record is 4,096 samples at 400 Hz; the underlying acquisitions were 7 s or 10 s, symmetrically zero-padded to that length.

cpsc-2018-china-physiological-signal-cha.name: CPSC 2018 (China Physiological Signal Challenge 2018)

schema_org.description: The public training set of the China Physiological Signal Challenge 2018, "Automatic identification of the rhythm/morphology abnormalities in 12-lead ECGs": 6,877 twelve-lead recordings collected at 11 Chinese hospitals, sampled at 500 Hz. Records are labelled with one normal and eight abnormal classes — AF, first-degree AV block, LBBB, RBBB, PAC, PVC, ST depression and ST elevation — and 476 of them carry more than one, so the task is multi-label. Record length varies from 6 s to 144 s (median 12 s), which is unusual for a 12-lead resting dataset and means a fixed window has to be sized to the shortest record. Age and sex are in the WFDB headers. No metadata file ships; CPSC2018Splitter builds one from the headers on first run.

ecg-capable-smartwatches-dataset.name: ECG-Capable Smartwatches Dataset

alternateName: Electrocardiogram-Capable Smartwatches: Assessing Their Clinical Accuracy and Application

creator.name: Complutense University of Madrid / Hospital Universitario Ramón y Cajal

schema_org.description: 915 electrocardiograms of a METRON PS-440 patient simulator, recorded simultaneously by a Philips TC30 hospital electrocardiograph used as the clinical reference and by four ECG-capable consumer smartwatches — Apple Watch Series 9, Samsung Galaxy Watch 6, Fitbit Sense 2 and Withings ScanWatch — following the accuracy protocol of IEC 60601-2-25:2011. The simulator was stepped through 36 calibrated settings in four families: heart rate from 30 to 300 bpm in 15 steps, R-wave amplitude at 500, 1000, 1500 and 2000 µV, ST-segment elevation and depression from -800 to +800 µV in 100 µV steps, and a 2 Hz square wave, each recorded five times on every device. The watches were held on an adjustable stand with the simulator's right-arm output wired to the crown and its left-arm output to the caseback, giving an arm-to-arm lead I; the electrocardiograph was connected with standard 12-lead cables and captured all twelve derivations. No person was recorded: every waveform is synthetic, which makes this the one release in ECGBench whose ground truth is an instrument setting known exactly rather than a clinical label, and therefore the natural place to measure what a wrist-worn device does to amplitude, rate and ST morphology.

ecg-effects-of-dofetilide-moxifloxacin-a.name: ECG Effects of Dofetilide, Moxifloxacin and Combinations (ECGDMMLD)

creator.name: US FDA / CDER; Phase I Crossover Study (NCT02308748)

schema_org.description: 4,211 ten-second 12-lead ECGs at 1 kHz (up-sampled from a 500 Hz acquisition) from 22 healthy volunteers in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 5-period crossover Phase I trial (study SCR-003, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02308748) run by the US FDA to test whether blocking late sodium current can shorten the QT prolongation produced by a selective hERG blocker. Every subject passed through all five arms in one of ten randomised sequences: dofetilide alone, dofetilide with mexiletine, dofetilide with lidocaine, moxifloxacin with diltiazem, and placebo. Within each period the drugs were staged hours apart, so the late-sodium or calcium blocker circulates alone before the hERG blocker joins it. Triplicate 10 s segments were extracted at 14 nominal timepoints from half an hour before dosing to 24 hours after, each paired with a plasma concentration sample, and each is published both as the raw 10 s segment and as a derived 16-channel median beat carrying semi-automatic P-onset, QRS-onset, QRS-offset, T-peak and T-offset annotations on the vector-magnitude lead. Per-record RR, PR, QT, QRS, J-Tpeak, Tpeak-Tend, early and late repolarisation durations and three T-wave morphology scores accompany the waveforms, alongside subject demographics. No participant had cardiac disease: the label of interest is drug exposure, not diagnosis.
schema_org.name: ECG Effects of Dofetilide, Moxifloxacin and Combinations (ECGDMMLD)

ecg-id-database.name: ECG-ID Database

schema_org.description: 310 single-lead ECG recordings from 90 volunteers, collected by Tatiana Lugovaya at the Electrotechnical University "LETI", Saint Petersburg, for her 2005 master's thesis on biometric human identification from the electrocardiogram. Each record is 20 seconds of Lead I — the left-hand minus right-hand potential, taken with limb clamp electrodes in the sitting position — digitised at 500 Hz, and each is stored as two channels: the raw signal, with every filter in the cardiograph software deliberately turned off, and the thesis's own filtered version of it (level-9 db8 wavelet baseline-drift removal, an adaptive 50 Hz bandstop, and a 5th-order Butterworth lowpass at 40 Hz). Subjects are students, colleagues and friends of the author — 44 men and 46 women aged 13 to 75 — and contribute 1 to 22 records each; 20 of the 90 were recorded on more than one of the ten acquisition days, Person_02 across six sessions spanning 156 days, which is what makes the database usable for studying whether an ECG biometric persists over time. Ten beats per record carry unaudited automatic R- and T-peak annotations. Age, sex and recording date are given per record in the header comments; there are no diagnoses.
schema_org.name: ECG-ID Database

schema_org.description: 100,000 12-lead ECGs from Columbia University Irving Medical Center and Allen Hospital, each paired with structural heart disease labels derived from a matched echocardiogram. schema_org.description: The reference open repository for electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI): 26 experiments contributed by ten institutions, pairing body-surface potential maps with simultaneously recorded cardiac-surface potentials and matched geometry. ECGBench indexes the 2,943 time-signal recordings of the 24 experiments that publish any, from 20 subjects — 13 human (three ventricular pacing-site studies from Prague with CARTO ground truth, a KIT PVC study, a Dalhousie paced/VT/VF study, two Valencia atrial-fibrillation patients mapped under adenosine AV block, five EP Solutions vest patients and one healthy Nijmegen subject recorded in a noisy and an MEG-shielded room), four animal (two Utah torso-tank ischaemia experiments with 599-electrode cage and 247-electrode sock plus 480 plunge needles, a Bordeaux torso-tank pig, a Maastricht closed-chest dog and an Auckland open-chest pig) and two simulated (Valencia atrial rotors, KIT ventricular pacing in five source models). Electrode counts run from 54 to 2,223 and sampling rates from 500 to 2,048 Hz. Geometry, transfer matrices and imaging ship alongside on the portal and are not indexed here.

european-st-t-database-edb.name: European ST-T Database (EDB)

creator.name: CNR Institute of Clinical Physiology, Pisa; European Society of Cardiology

schema_org.description: 90 annotated two-hour excerpts of ambulatory ECG from 79 subjects (70 men aged 30-84, 8 women, information missing for one), each with diagnosed or suspected myocardial ischaemia. Assembled between 1985 and 1990 by a European Society of Cardiology concerted action across centres in seven countries, coordinated by the CNR Institute of Clinical Physiology in Pisa, and selected to give a representative spread of ECG abnormality rather than to sample any population. Each record holds two signals at 250 Hz with 12-bit resolution over a nominal 20 mV range, rescaled after digitisation to a uniform 200 ADC units per millivolt. Two cardiologists annotated every record beat by beat and marked the onset, extremum and end of each interval of significant ST-segment or T-wave change in each signal independently, applying predefined criteria — 0.1 mV of ST deviation or 0.2 mV of T deviation, sustained for at least 30 s, measured against a reference waveform from that record's first 30 seconds. Disagreements were resolved by the coordinating group. The reference annotation files hold 802,909 annotations in total, including 790,565 beats, 368 ST episodes and 401 T episodes, with peak displacements from 100 uV to more than 1 mV.
schema_org.name: European ST-T Database (EDB)

eye-tracking-dataset-for-12-lead-ecg-int.name: Eye Tracking Dataset for 12-Lead ECG Interpretation

creator.name: Qatar Biomedical Research Institute, Hamad bin Khalifa Univ.

schema_org.description:
This release measures **how clinicians read an ECG**, not what an ECG
contains. Sixty-three practitioners — from junior medical students to
board-certified consultants — were each shown the same ten printed 12-lead
ECGs for about 30 seconds apiece while an eye tracker recorded where they
looked. What ships is the aggregated gaze behaviour:

- **`Datasets/Grid_Anonymized.csv`** — 14,742 rows, one per reader x image x
  area of interest, where the areas are the individual lead boxes, the
  quarters of each rhythm strip, and the printed settings footer.
- **`Datasets/Long_Short_Anonymized.csv`** — the same 630 sessions scored
  against a two-region split instead: `Long` (the rhythm strips) versus
  `Short` (the twelve short lead traces).
- **`ECGs/ECG_Images/`** — the ten stimulus images (JPG/PNG).
- **`AOI_Distributions/`** — two figures showing how the AOI grids were laid
  out over the normal-sinus-rhythm image.

Each row carries 17 gaze and fixation measures: time to first hit, total and
percentage dwell time, revisit counts, fixation counts and durations. The
research use is expertise modelling and attention prediction — which lead
draws the eye first, and how that changes between a medical student and a
consultant.
schema_org.name: Eye Tracking Dataset for 12-Lead ECG Interpretation

ikem-dataset-institute-for-clinical-and-.name: IKEM Dataset (Institute for Clinical and Experimental Medicine, Prague)

creator.name: IKEM (Institute for Clinical and Experimental Medicine)

schema_org.description: 98,130 twelve-lead ECGs from 30,290 patients recorded at the Institute for Clinical and Experimental Medicine (IKEM) in Prague, Czech Republic, mostly in 2017-2018 with a tail running 2004-2022. Each recording is 4,096 samples at 500 Hz (8.192 s), stored as int16 microvolts. Only 8 of the 12 leads are kept — V1-V6, II and I, in that order — because the other four are exact linear combinations of II and I and can be recomputed; ECGBench returns the 8 stored leads as they are. The release ships demographics and two cart-measured rates rather than diagnoses: age, sex, weight, height, ventricular rate and atrial rate, with -1 used as a missing-value sentinel throughout. Patients repeat heavily — 19,078 of the 30,290 contributed more than one recording and one contributed 96, covering 86,918 of the 98,130 records — so folds are grouped on patient_id.
schema_org.name: IKEM Dataset (Institute for Clinical and Experimental Medicine, Prague)

schema_org.description:
**The authors have asked for downloads of KURIAS-ECG to be disabled until
further notice**, following an internal audit at the Korea University Medical
Center. The PhysioNet project page may still resolve, but the data are not
obtainable from it.

This is why the status above reads *Unavailable* rather than *Not started*:
the dataset is not waiting on work from ECGBench. Nothing here can make it
loadable while the source is withdrawn, so it has no config, no fold
assignment and nothing on the HuggingFace Hub — and will not until the authors
restore access.

The entry is kept in the catalogue deliberately rather than deleted. The
figures above describe the release as it was published, so a paper citing
KURIAS-ECG can still be placed against it, and anyone holding a copy from
before the suspension knows what they have.

Check the PhysioNet project page for the current position; ECGBench does not
track it automatically.
schema_org.name: KURIAS-ECG

leipzig-heart-center-ecg-database.name: Leipzig Heart Center ECG Database

schema_org.description: The Leipzig Heart Center ECG Database: 39 annotated recordings from electrophysiological studies at the Leipzig Heart Center, covering arrhythmias in children and in patients with congenital heart disease. 29 children (x001-x0029) presented with AV reentrant or AV nodal reentrant tachycardia; 10 adults (x100-x109) had repaired Tetralogy of Fallot, 8 of them with ventricular tachycardia. Every record holds the 12-lead surface ECG together with intracardiac electrograms from a coronary sinus catheter, a right-ventricular apex catheter and an ablation catheter, sampled at 977 Hz with a gain of 2000/mV, and a cardiologist's beat, rhythm and signal-quality annotations in a companion .atr. Note that the channel count is not constant — 14, 18, 19 or 20 depending on which catheters were in place — and that only the first 12 channels are the same channel in every record.
schema_org.name: Leipzig Heart Center ECG Database

long-term-af-database-ltafdb.name: Long-Term AF Database (LTAFDB)

schema_org.description: 84 long-term ECG recordings of subjects with paroxysmal or sustained atrial fibrillation, contributed by Steven Swiryn and colleagues at Northwestern University and digitised at Boston's Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. Each record holds two simultaneously recorded ECG signals at 128 Hz with 12-bit resolution over a 20 mV range; the headers name both channels "ECG" and state no electrode placement. Durations vary from 6.1 to 26.4 hours and are typically 24-25, giving 1,960.6 hours in total. The reference `.atr` annotations — 8,995,973 typed beats and 53,704 rhythm episodes in nine codes — were produced by MEDICALgorithmics' PocketECG algorithm and manually verified by their ECG technicians, and contributed to PhysioNet in 2012. Unaudited `sqrs` detections ship alongside them in `.qrs`, together with 81 hand-placed markers for spontaneous AF terminations, which are what the AF Termination Challenge Database's one-minute excerpts were cut around.
schema_org.name: Long-Term AF Database (LTAFDB)

long-term-st-database-ltstdb.name: Long-Term ST Database (LTSTDB)

creator.name: University of Ljubljana; CNR Institute of Clinical Physiology, Pisa; MIT

schema_org.description: 86 continuous ambulatory ECG recordings from 80 subjects, each 17 to 48 hours long (median 23.4 h, 1,992 hours in total), assembled between 1995 and 2002 by an inter-institutional collaboration coordinated by the University of Ljubljana with the CNR Institute of Clinical Physiology in Pisa and MIT. The recordings were chosen to exhibit a variety of ST segment events — ischaemic episodes, axis-related non-ischaemic episodes, episodes of slow ST level drift and mixtures of these — so that a detector can be scored on telling them apart rather than merely on finding deviation. Each record holds two or three signals at 250 Hz with 12-bit resolution over a nominal 20 mV range. Expert annotators at all three sites reviewed every record independently with the SEMIA tool, marking the isoelectric level and J point on 16-second averaged cardiac cycles, placing the local references that define a piecewise-linear baseline ST level function, and then annotating each ST episode against the resulting deviation function; consensus reference annotations were agreed at meetings held several times a year. The release ships 8,897,780 manually corrected beat annotations, three sets of ST episode annotations under different detection criteria, ST level measurements at eight points of every beat, and Karhunen-Loeve and Legendre coefficient time series derived from the ST segments.
schema_org.name: Long-Term ST Database (LTSTDB)

creator.name: Medical Univ. of Graz; KIT; PTB; Univ. of Edinburgh

schema_org.description: 16,842 synthetic 12-lead ECGs produced by multi-scale electrophysiological simulation rather than recorded from people. Atrial and ventricular models were run independently on 13 anatomical/electrophysiological model configurations, composed into 10 s rhythms at 500 Hz and projected onto torso models. Eight pathology classes ship — normal sinus rhythm, AV block, left and right bundle branch block, left atrial enlargement, fibrotic atrial cardiomyopathy, interatrial conduction block, and myocardial infarction, the last split into eight subclasses by occlusion site (LAD/LCX/RCA), transmurality (0.3 or 1.0) and, for LCX, anterior or posterior region. Every record ships three times: noise-free simulator output, the same with superimposed noise, and a 0.5-150 Hz filtered version. The full simulation parameter set — ion model, conductivities, action potential durations, stimulus sites, electrode positions, atrial geometry and torso — ships per record and is exposed through the label loader.

mhd-effect-on-12-lead-ecgs-in-mri-scanne.name: MHD Effect on 12-Lead ECGs in MRI Scanners

alternateName: MHD Effect on 12-Lead and 3-Lead ECGs in MRI Scanners
schema_org.description: 53 ECG records from 26 healthy volunteers, acquired in 1T, 3T and 7T MRI scanners at Otto-von-Guericke University Magdeburg between 2011 and 2017, all at 1024 Hz. Inside the bore the magnetohydrodynamic effect — induced by blood flowing through the static B0 field — superimposes a voltage large enough to obscure the P wave, ST segment and T wave, which is what makes ECG-based patient monitoring and gating hard during MRI exams. Recordings were made without imaging, so no switched gradient or RF fields contribute and the distortion is MHD alone. 10 records are reference ECGs taken outside the scanner for the same subjects, standing in for the unobtainable in-bore ground truth. 39 records are diagnostic 12-lead on a Getemed CM 3000 Holter; 14 are 3-lead (I, II, III) on an MRI-conditional MIPM Tesla M3 monitor. Every QRS complex was manually annotated by physicians or ECG experts — 14,950 in total, with no distinction between normal and ectopic beats — and no subject had a known cardiac disease. The 1T scanner was an open-bore Philips Panorama HFO whose B0 is *vertical* (back to chest) rather than horizontal, so its records were made prone and supine to invert the MHD effect; every other scanner is horizontal-B0 and was used head-first and feet-first, supine.
schema_org.name: MHD Effect on 12-Lead ECGs in MRI Scanners

schema_org.description:
MIMIC-IV-ECG-Ext-ICD is a **label layer, not a standalone dataset**: it ships
no waveforms. It is one 323 MB table, `records_w_diag_icd10.csv`, whose
800,035 rows are exactly the 800,035 studies of
[MIMIC-IV-ECG]({{ site.baseurl }}/datasets/mimic-iv-ecg.html), keyed by that
dataset's own `study_id`.

What it adds is **clinical ground truth**, which MIMIC-IV-ECG itself lacks:
ICD-10-CM discharge diagnoses linked from the MIMIC-IV emergency-department
and hospital modules. MIMIC-IV-ECG's own labels are the ECG cart's automated
report — the machine's opinion of the trace. These are what the patient was
discharged with, which makes it possible to train an ECG model against
conditions no ECG algorithm reports on.

Five diagnosis columns are shipped, differing in where the codes came from:

- **`ed_diag_ed`** — ED discharge diagnoses, from the MIMIC-IV-ED module.
- **`ed_diag_hosp`** — hospital discharge diagnoses, reached via `ed_hadm_id`.
- **`hosp_diag_hosp`** — hospital discharge diagnoses, reached via `hosp_hadm_id`.
- **`all_diag_hosp`** — the previous two, de-duplicated.
- **`all_diag_all`** — `all_diag_hosp` where it exists, otherwise `ed_diag_ed`.
  **This is the one to train on**, and the one the published benchmark uses.

Alongside them come patient demographics, date of death, the linkage ids that
produced the join, and the release's own 20-fold patient-grouped split.

Access is **credentialed** under the PhysioNet DUA — the same agreement as
MIMIC-IV-ECG — so ECGBench never redistributes these codes.
schema_org.name: MIMIC-IV-ECG-Ext-ICD

mit-bih-arrhythmia-database.name: MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database

schema_org.description: 48 half-hour excerpts of two-channel ambulatory ECG, digitised at 360 Hz from Holter tapes recorded at the Beth Israel Hospital Arrhythmia Laboratory between 1975 and 1979. 23 records (100-124) were chosen at random from a set of over 4000 recordings to be representative of routine clinical material; the other 25 (200-234) were selected to include rare but clinically important phenomena that a small random sample would not contain. Each record carries reference annotations independently marked by two cardiologists and resolved by consensus: 109,494 beats across fifteen types, plus rhythm episodes, signal quality changes and artefact markers. The upper signal is usually a modified limb lead II and the lower a modified V1, but not always, and in record 114 the two are reversed.

mit-bih-atrial-fibrillation-database.name: MIT-BIH Atrial Fibrillation Database

schema_org.description: 25 long-term ECG recordings from human subjects with atrial fibrillation, mostly paroxysmal, recorded at Beth Israel Hospital in Boston and digitised at 250 Hz with 12-bit resolution over a 20 mV range. Each record holds two ECG signals, named ECG1 and ECG2 in the headers with no statement of which anatomical leads they are, and runs 10 h 13.7 min; one (06453) stops at 9 h 15 min. The reference annotations are rhythm episodes in four codes — atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, AV junctional rhythm, and N for everything else — manually reviewed, 623 episodes covering 254.7 hours in total. Unaudited automatic beat annotations ship for all 25 records (1,221,559 detections) and manually corrected beat annotations for two of them. Two records, 00735 and 03665, ship annotations but no signal files.
schema_org.name: MIT-BIH Atrial Fibrillation Database

mit-bih-normal-sinus-rhythm-database.name: MIT-BIH Normal Sinus Rhythm Database

schema_org.description: 18 long-term two-lead ECG recordings of subjects referred to the Arrhythmia Laboratory at Boston's Beth Israel Hospital (now Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center) who were found to have had no significant arrhythmias — 5 men aged 26 to 45 and 13 women aged 20 to 50. Each record is a full day of ambulatory Holter, 23.13 h to 25.96 h, digitised at 128 Hz with 12-bit resolution; the two channels are named ECG1 and ECG2 in the headers with no statement of which anatomical leads they are. The reference annotations are beat labels and per-channel signal-quality transitions: 1,729,629 beats over 437.5 hours, of which 1,729,502 are normal, 91 supraventricular premature, 26 ventricular premature, 8 fusion and 2 nodal premature. There are no rhythm annotations and no diagnostic label — the whole database is one class, and that is what makes it the standard normal control and normal-HRV reference.
schema_org.name: MIT-BIH Normal Sinus Rhythm Database

mit-bih-st-change-database.name: MIT-BIH ST Change Database

schema_org.description: 28 ECG recordings of varying lengths exhibiting transient ST change, collected by Paul Albrecht at MIT for his 1983 master's thesis on S-T segment characterization for long-term automated ECG analysis and published by PhysioNet in August 1999. Most were recorded during exercise stress tests and show transient ST depression; the last five (323 through 327) are excerpts of long-term ECG recordings and show ST elevation. Each record is digitised at 360 Hz with 12-bit resolution and runs 13.1 to 67.2 minutes, for 13.49 hours in total, and no two records are the same length. Eighteen records hold two channels and ten hold one; every channel is described in every header only as "ECG", with no electrode placement stated. The accompanying reference annotations are beat labels only — 76,175 beats among 76,181 annotations, 75,038 of them normal — and the release deliberately carries no ST change annotations, unlike the European ST-T Database. No subject-level information ships in any form: the headers have no comment line, and there is no age, sex, diagnosis or subject identifier anywhere in the 142 files.
schema_org.name: MIT-BIH ST Change Database

mit-bih-supraventricular-arrhythmia-data.name: MIT-BIH Supraventricular Arrhythmia Database

schema_org.description: 78 half-hour two-channel ambulatory ECG recordings, digitised at 128 Hz, chosen to supplement the examples of supraventricular arrhythmia in the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database. The reference annotations are beat labels: 184,583 beats, of which 162,339 are normal, 12,188 supraventricular premature, 9,943 ventricular premature, 79 unclassifiable, 23 fusion, 9 nodal premature, 1 aberrated atrial premature and 1 bundle branch block. Alongside them are 2,211 isolated-artifact markers and 1,082 per-channel signal-quality transitions, which between them mark 2.59% of the recorded time as noisy on at least one channel. The two channels are named ECG1 and ECG2 in the headers with no statement of which anatomical leads they are, and the release ships no demographics, no subject identifiers and no diagnoses. Beat annotation covers essentially the whole of every record.
schema_org.name: MIT-BIH Supraventricular Arrhythmia Database

schema_org.description: 12-lead surface ECGs from 334 patients who underwent successful catheter ablation for outflow-tract ventricular arrhythmia at Ningbo First Hospital, recorded intra-procedurally on an EP-WorkMate system at 2000 Hz. Each patient's label is the origin the ablation confirmed — right (257) or left (77) outflow tract, and one of 12 anatomic sub-sites within it — so the ground truth is invasive rather than an ECG reading, and the task is to predict the origin from the surface ECG before the procedure. Recordings are excerpts of the procedure containing both sinus beats and ectopy, so length varies from 2.9 s to 59 s. Two directories ship: raw integers (canonical) and a wavelet-denoised copy. Sex is recorded; age is not.

norwegian-endurance-athlete-ecg-database.name: Norwegian Endurance Athlete ECG Database

schema_org.description: Twelve-lead resting ECGs from 28 elite Norwegian endurance athletes — 24 rowers, 2 kayakers and 2 cyclists, 19 men and 9 women aged 20-43, training roughly 800 hours a year — recorded at the University of Oslo in February and March 2020 on a GE MAC VUE 360. Each record is 10 seconds at 500 Hz and was interpreted twice: once by the GE Marquette SL12 algorithm (version 23, v243) and once by a cardiologist trained in athlete ECG interpretation using international criteria. Both readings ship as free-text comment lines in the WFDB header. The dataset exists to expose how badly general-purpose automated interpretation over-calls findings in hearts remodelled by endurance training; no echocardiography was performed, so athletic remodelling is not confirmed per athlete. Waveform amplitudes are per-lead normalised rather than calibrated — see the header comment above.
schema_org.name: Norwegian Endurance Athlete ECG Database

physionet-cinc-challenge-2017-af-classif.name: PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2017 (AF Classification)

schema_org.description: The public training set of the PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2017: 8,528 single-lead ECG recordings donated by AliveCor, each taken by a member of the public holding a handheld two-electrode device in their hands, so the trace is nominally a lead I equivalent. Recordings are 9-61 s long (typically 30 s) at 300 Hz, band-limited to 0.5-40 Hz. Each is labelled with exactly one of four rhythm classes — normal, atrial fibrillation, other rhythm, or too noisy to classify — which makes this the reference benchmark for AF detection from consumer single-lead ECG rather than from clinical 12-lead. The labels were revised twice during the competition using the entrants' own disagreement to find contentious records, and all four shipped label versions are exposed. No demographics and no patient identifier ship. The 3,658-record hidden test set was never released.
schema_org.name: PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2017 (AF Classification)

physionet-cinc-challenge-2020.name: PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2020

schema_org.description: The public training set of the 2020 PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge, "Classification of 12-lead ECGs": 43,101 12-lead ECG records pooled from six source cohorts across China, Russia, Germany and the USA, distributed in a single uniform WFDB tree. Diagnoses are multi-label SNOMED-CT codes in the per-record header (#Dx) — 111 distinct codes, 2.18 per record on average, of which 27 were scored by the challenge metric. Age and sex are in the headers too. Unusually for ECGBench, sampling rate (257/500/1000 Hz) and record length (5 s to 1800 s) both vary per record, so both are exposed as per-record labels rather than dataset constants. The 2021 challenge reuses this entire training set and adds two further cohorts.
schema_org.name: PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2020

post-ictal-heart-rate-oscillations-in-pa.name: Post-Ictal Heart Rate Oscillations in Partial Epilepsy

creator.name: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Harvard Medical School

schema_org.description: Seven single-lead ECG recordings, 1.50 h to 3.77 h each and 16.77 h in total, digitised at 200 Hz from continuous EEG/ECG/video epilepsy monitoring of five women aged 31 to 48 with partial seizures of frontal or temporal origin and no clinical evidence of cardiac disease, recorded at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center under a protocol approved by its Committee on Clinical Investigations. The accompanying paper reports transient low-frequency heart-rate oscillations (0.01-0.10 Hz, two to six minutes long, 15 to 41 bpm peak-to-trough) appearing immediately after five of 11 recorded seizures, one in each of the five patients, and absent from the pre-ictal period of those same seizures. The shipped `times.seize` file gives onset and offset for 10 of those seizures, read from simultaneous EEG by an electroencephalographer blinded to the heart-rate analysis; the EEG itself was not released. Each record also carries an uncorrected automated beat annotation file — 73,843 detections, of which 350 are the detector's learning phase, 183 ventricular and 196 supraventricular — plus 37 ST-change episodes and, in one record, 17.4 s of annotated atrial fibrillation. The release ships no subject identifier and no per-record demographics; the five-subject grouping ECGBench splits on is reconstructed from beat morphology and validated against the two counts the paper states.
schema_org.name: Post-Ictal Heart Rate Oscillations in Partial Epilepsy

preterm-infant-cardio-respiratory-signal.name: Preterm Infant Cardio-Respiratory Signals Database (PICSDB)

schema_org.description: Ten simultaneous ECG and respiration recordings — 439.8 hours of ECG, 20.3 h to 70.3 h per infant — collected at the bedside from Philips IntelliVue MP70 monitors in the neonatal intensive care unit of the University of Massachusetts Memorial Healthcare. The infants were 29 3/7 to 34 2/7 weeks post-conceptional age (mean 31 1/7) and 843 to 2,100 g at study (mean 1,468), all spontaneously breathing room air, none with congenital or perinatal CNS infection, intraventricular haemorrhage of grade II or above, or hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy. A single ECG channel was recorded at 500 Hz for eight infants and as a 250 Hz compound signal for the other two; respiration was measured with inductance bands around the chest wall and abdomen, at 50 Hz for nine infants and 500 Hz for one, synchronised to the ECG by the VueLogger acquisition software. The database was published to support prediction of bradycardia, and its ground truth is 622 manually validated bradycardia onsets — heart rate below 100 bpm for at least two beats — alongside 3,797,503 R peaks located by a modified Pan-Tompkins detector and visually inspected for artefact. The respiration peaks were extracted algorithmically and, unlike the other two layers, were never manually vetted.
schema_org.name: Preterm Infant Cardio-Respiratory Signals Database (PICSDB)

schema_org.description: 549 ECG records from 290 subjects recorded at the Benjamin Franklin University Clinic, Berlin. schema_org.description:
PTB-XL+ is a **companion release, not a standalone dataset**: it ships no raw
ECGs. It annotates the same 21,799 recordings PTB-XL holds, keyed by PTB-XL's
own `ecg_id`, and its value is that it gives several independent opinions
about each recording:

- **`labels/ptbxl_statements.csv`** — PTB-XL's cardiologist-assigned SCP
  statements, extended with SNOMED CT concept ids.
- **`labels/12sl_statements.csv`** — statements from the Marquette 12SL
  commercial algorithm, likewise SNOMED-mapped. Comparing human against
  algorithm on identical recordings is much of the point.
- **`features/{unig,ecgdeli,12sl}_features.csv`** — 748, 531 and 782 measured
  features from three independent providers (University of Glasgow, the KIT
  ECGdeli toolbox, Marquette 12SL), with `features/feature_description.csv`
  mapping equivalent columns between them.
- **`fiducial_points/ecgdeli/`** — 283,326 per-lead WFDB annotation files.
- **`median_beats/{12sl,unig}/`** — derived single-beat waveforms. See the
  defects below; ECGBench exposes these as paths only.

Everything is CC BY 4.0, so unlike MIMIC-IV-ECG there is no redistribution
question here.
schema_org.name: PTB-XL+

qt-database-qtdb.name: QT Database (QTDB)

creator.name: Universidad de Zaragoza; MIT; Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center

schema_org.description: 105 fifteen-minute two-channel ECG excerpts, sampled at 250 Hz, in which expert cardiologists manually marked the onset, peak and end of the P wave, the onset and end of the QRS complex, the peak and end of the T wave and — where present — the peak and end of the U wave, for 3,623 individually selected beats. It was built at MIT and the University of Zaragoza in 1997 to give QT-measurement algorithms a reference they had never had, and it remains the standard benchmark for ECG delineation. The excerpts were chosen to span a wide range of QRS and ST-T morphology and to avoid baseline wander, which biases them toward lower heart rates; they were drawn from six existing databases plus 24 Holter recordings from Beth Israel Hospital patients who died suddenly during recording and their matched controls. At least 30 consecutive beats of the dominant morphology were annotated per record, plus up to 20 of each non-dominant morphology, and only beats ARISTOTLE classified as normal with normal neighbours were eligible. Annotation was confined to the final five minutes of each excerpt so that an algorithm has ten minutes of learning data ahead of it. Eleven records carry a second, independent set of annotations for inter-observer studies. Automatic boundaries from ecgpuwave ship alongside, covering every beat of every record, unaudited.
schema_org.name: QT Database (QTDB)

sami-trop-chagas-cardiomyopathy-cohort.name: SaMi-Trop (Chagas Cardiomyopathy Cohort)

schema_org.description: 1,631 twelve-lead ECGs — the first exam of each of 1,631 patients — from SaMi-Trop, an NIH-funded prospective cohort of patients with chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy recruited in Minas Gerais, Brazil, and followed for mortality. Recordings are 4,096 samples at 400 Hz (10.24 s), zero-padded from acquisitions of 7-10 s. The release ships no diagnostic label vocabulary: what it carries instead is age, sex, a single `normal_ecg` flag, a neural-network age estimate, and — the reason the dataset exists — complete mortality follow-up, with 104 of the 1,631 patients dead within a median 2.07 years. Every patient contributes exactly one recording, so there is no patient grouping to do and no within-dataset leakage to avoid.

shandong-provincial-hospital-ecg-databas.name: Shandong Provincial Hospital ECG Database (SPHDB)

schema_org.description: 25,770 twelve-lead clinical ECGs from 24,666 patients recorded at Shandong Provincial Hospital between August 2019 and August 2020, sampled at 500 Hz and stored one HDF5 array per record. Its distinguishing feature is the labelling: diagnoses are AHA/ACC/HRS standardised statements — 44 primary statements in 11 categories plus 15 modifiers — rather than a dataset-specific vocabulary, so a record's ground truth reads as "60+310;147" (frequent ventricular premature complexes, T-wave abnormality). 3,724 records (14.45%) carry more than one statement and 46.05% carry an abnormality. Record length varies from 10 s to 56 s, and the metadata's N column gives it exactly, so a fixed window has to be sized to the shortest record. Age (18-95) and sex are complete for every row.

schema_org.description: 128 twenty-four-hour Holter recordings from 122 Japanese adults who underwent ambulatory monitoring at Saitama Medical University International Medical Center between May 2019 and May 2023, published to give AF research a Japanese cohort where MITDB, AFDB, LTAFDB, IRIDIA-AF, Icentia11k and CPSC2021 offer none. Two channels were recorded on a Fukuda Holter monitor at 125 Hz — ECG1 a modified CC5 lead, ECG2 a NASA lead — then band-passed at [0.67-100] Hz and resampled to 200 Hz. 98 of the recordings carry rhythm annotations placed beat by beat in PhysioZoo by a cardiology fellow, covering atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, atrial tachycardia and other supraventricular tachycardias; normal sinus rhythm and everything else was deliberately left unlabelled, so the `N` code is a residual class rather than a sinus-rhythm label. R-peak positions for all 128 recordings come from the epltd implementation of Pan-Tompkins and are unaudited. AdditionalData.csv adds 45 columns of clinical and demographic data per recording — diagnosis, comorbidity, medication, echocardiography and ablation history — which makes this one of very few Holter releases where record-level clinical context and time-resolved rhythm labels ship together.
schema_org.name: SHDB-AF (Saitama Holter Database — Atrial Fibrillation)

st-petersburg-incart-12-lead-arrhythmia-.name: St Petersburg INCART 12-Lead Arrhythmia Database

creator.name: St. Petersburg Institute of Cardiological Technics (INCART)

schema_org.description: 75 annotated recordings extracted from 32 Holter records, collected at the St Petersburg Institute of Cardiological Technics from patients undergoing tests for coronary artery disease. Each record is 30 minutes of 12 standard leads at 257 Hz. Preference was given to subjects whose ECGs were consistent with ischaemia, coronary artery disease, conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias; none had pacemakers and most had ventricular ectopic beats. The reference annotation files carry 175,907 beat labels across ten beat types, produced by an automatic algorithm and then corrected manually. Per-record ECG findings and per-patient diagnoses are stored in the WFDB header comments.
schema_org.name: St Petersburg INCART 12-Lead Arrhythmia Database

st-vincent-s-ucd-sleep-apnea-database-uc.name: St. Vincent's / UCD Sleep Apnea Database (UCDDB)

alternateName: St. Vincent's University Hospital / University College Dublin Sleep Apnea Database

creator.name: St. Vincent's University Hospital / University College Dublin

schema_org.description: 25 full overnight polysomnograms with simultaneous three-channel Holter ECG, from adults referred to the Sleep Disorders Clinic at St Vincent's University Hospital, Dublin, for suspected obstructive sleep apnea, central sleep apnea or primary snoring. Subjects were selected at random over six months from September 2002 to February 2003 and had to be over 18, free of known cardiac disease and autonomic dysfunction, and not on medication affecting heart rate: 21 men and 4 women, aged 50 +/- 10 years (28 to 68), BMI 31.6 +/- 4.0 kg/m2, apnea-hypopnea index 24.1 +/- 20.3 (1.7 to 90.9). The Holter recordings ECGBench splits are V5, CC5 and V5R at 128 Hz from a Reynolds Lifecard CF, 7.52 h to 8.68 h each and 203.4 h in all. Each study also ships a 14-channel polysomnogram, 20,789 sleep epochs scored to Rechtschaffen and Kales rules by an experienced sleep technologist, and 3,428 respiratory events (obstructive, central and mixed apneas and hypopneas, plus periodic breathing) annotated by the same scorer with duration, oxygen desaturation, snoring, arousal and heart-rate change.
schema_org.name: St. Vincent's / UCD Sleep Apnea Database (UCDDB)

staff-iii-database.name: STAFF III Database

creator.name: Charleston Area Medical Center; Lund University

schema_org.description: 520 standard-lead ECG recordings from 104 patients undergoing prolonged elective percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA) at Charleston Area Medical Center, West Virginia, recorded 1995-1996. Each patient contributed a short series of recordings around a single procedure: a baseline on the ward, a baseline in the catheterisation laboratory, one or more recordings during balloon inflation, and recoveries in both locations. The 142 balloon-inflation records carry 152 sample-accurate inflation and deflation markers plus 210 contrast-injection markers, and the occluded vessel is recorded for every inflation. Because occlusion is deliberate, timed and performed with the patient as their own control, the dataset is the reference set for transient-ischaemia and ST-change work. Signals are nine leads (V1-V6, I, II, III) at 1,000 Hz with 0.625 uV resolution.
schema_org.name: STAFF III Database

sudden-cardiac-death-holter-database.name: Sudden Cardiac Death Holter Database

schema_org.description: 23 complete long-term Holter recordings of patients who sustained a ventricular tachyarrhythmia during the recording and, in most cases, an actual cardiac arrest. The recordings were made mainly in the 1980s in Boston-area hospitals and collected by Scott Greenwald at MIT, then compiled as part of a study of ventricular arrhythmias; PhysioNet released them in 2004 as the first sudden cardiac death database. Each record is two channels digitised from analog Holter tape at 250 Hz with 12-bit resolution, running 3.93 h to 25.14 h for 446.6 hours in total, and no two records are the same length. Both channels are described in every header only as "ECG", with no statement of electrode placement. The cohort is 18 subjects with underlying sinus rhythm (4 of them intermittently paced), 1 continuously paced and 4 in atrial fibrillation, aged 17 to 89 where an age was recorded at all. The onset of the terminal arrhythmia is given as an elapsed time in a header comment for 20 of the 23 records, and it is the only clinical annotation the files carry. Two annotation layers ship: unaudited detector output for all 23 records, 1,888,495 beats, and an explicitly incomplete audited reference set for 12 of them, 849,831 beats. Because the collection is retrospective, patient information is limited and sometimes absent entirely, including drug regimens and doses.
schema_org.name: Sudden Cardiac Death Holter Database

Symile-MIMIC is a **multimodal cohort over MIMIC-IV-ECG's recordings, not a

three modalities drawn from MIMIC-IV:

- a **12-lead ECG** taken within 24 h of admission, from
  [MIMIC-IV-ECG]({{ site.baseurl }}/datasets/mimic-iv-ecg.html) — 10 s at
  500 Hz, 5,000 samples per lead;
- a **chest X-ray** taken in the 24–72 h window post-admission, from
  MIMIC-CXR-JPG, with the 14 CheXpert findings for it;
- up to **50 blood labs** drawn within 24 h of admission, from MIMIC-IV hosp.

It was built for the NeurIPS 2024 Symile paper, whose contrastive objective
needs three or more modalities at once, and its evaluation task is **CXR
retrieval**: given a query's ECG and labs, pick that query's chest X-ray out
of 10 candidates. Only admissions with all three modalities present — and a
PA or AP view, and at least one of the 50 labs — qualified, which is why
11,622 admissions come out of MIMIC-IV-ECG's 800,035 studies.

Access is **credentialed** under the PhysioNet Credentialed Health Data Use
Agreement — the same agreement as MIMIC-IV-ECG — so ECGBench redistributes
none of it.
schema_org.name: Symile-MIMIC

toliet-thigh-based-ecg-toilet-seat.name: tOLIet (Thigh-based ECG, toilet seat)

alternateName: tOLIet (Thigh-based ECG from a Toilet Seat)

creator.name: Centro Hospitalar Universitário de Lisboa Central (CHULC)

schema_org.description: Single-lead electrocardiograms acquired at the thighs by an "invisible" ECG system built into a toilet seat: 145 sittings by 86 volunteers at the Centro Hospitalar Universitario de Lisboa Central, each recorded simultaneously by four polymeric dry-electrode pairs embedded in the seat that differ only in surface texture — flat, sinusoidal, pyramidal and trapezoidal. The release is therefore a controlled comparison of electrode geometry under the hardest realistic condition: dry skin, no gel, no preparation, and whatever contact a seated person happens to make. ECGBench exposes each electrode channel as its own single-lead record, giving 580 records of which 342 carry a signal; the rest are pairs that made no contact and are kept in the `original` version only. Signals are 1 kHz, 10-bit over a ±1.5 mV span, band-limited 0.5-40 Hz in hardware, and run 14.4 s to 197.2 s. 23 of the sittings have a simultaneous clinical 12-lead resting ECG as ground truth. Age, weight, height and sex ship per subject; four sittings carry a paroxysmal atrial fibrillation note and the rest carry no diagnosis at all.
schema_org.name: tOLIet (Thigh-based ECG, toilet seat)

schema_org.description:
Intraoperative arrhythmia, annotated by the people who manage it. Five
anesthesiologists reviewed screened stretches of Lead II from 482 surgical
cases at Seoul National University Hospital, labelling every beat and every
rhythm segment, with each segment read independently by at least two of them
(reported Cohen's kappa 0.930 ± 0.130). Public ECG arrhythmia data is
overwhelmingly ambulatory Holter or ICU telemetry; this is the operating
theatre, where surgical stimulus, anesthetic agents and autonomic swings
produce a different mix of rhythms and a different noise profile.

**The release ships no ECG waveforms.** What you download from PhysioNet is
a `metadata.csv` and 482 per-case annotation CSVs. The signals live in the
public [VitalDB](https://vitaldb.net/) project and are fetched by `case_id`:

```python
import vitaldb
vals = vitaldb.load_case(1018, ['SNUADC/ECG_II'], 1/500)
```

Both halves are open — CC BY 4.0 here, and VitalDB needs no credentialing —
so this is a packaging split, not an access restriction. But it does mean
the annotations and the samples arrive by different routes.
schema_org.name: VitalDB Arrhythmia Database

wilson-central-terminal-ecg-database.name: Wilson Central Terminal ECG Database

creator.name: MARCS Institute, Western Sydney Univ.; Campbelltown Hospital

schema_org.description: Simultaneous conventional and true-unipolar 12-lead-style ECGs from 92 patients admitted to Campbelltown Hospital, Sydney, recorded so that the Wilson Central Terminal could be measured instead of assumed to be zero. Each of the 540 ten-second segments holds 37 channels at 800 Hz: the bipolar limb leads I, II, III, the precordial leads V1-V6, the three limb electrode potentials LA, RA and LL, the six true unipolar chest leads UV1-UV6 and the WCT itself — each of the first 18 present both raw and after DC removal plus a 0.05-150 Hz band-pass. The cohort is elderly and cardiac (mean age 65.2, SD 12.1; 27 of 92 female), with one free-text admission diagnosis per patient and no beat-level annotation. Eight segments from five patients carry precordial channels synthesised as V = UV - WCT rather than recorded.

zzu-pecg-zhengzhou-university-pediatric-.name: ZZU pECG (Zhengzhou University Pediatric ECG Database)

creator.name: First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University

schema_org.description: 14,190 paediatric ECGs from 11,643 hospitalised children at the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University, China, recorded between 2018 and 2024 at 500 Hz. Ages run from 1 day to 15.0 years (median 8.6 years), which makes this the only genuinely paediatric 12-lead resource in the catalogue — age-appropriate ECG interpretation differs substantially from adult interpretation, so adult-trained models should not be assumed to transfer. Records are 5-120 s long and store either 12 leads (12,334) or 9 (1,856, without V2/V4/V6). Labels are unusually rich for an open release: every record carries one or more ECG findings coded in both the AHA and Chinese vocabularies with human-readable descriptions, a list of ICD-10 discharge diagnoses, and three per-lead signal-quality indices. 3,716 records carry one of the 19 studied cardiovascular ICD-10 codes, grouped as congenital heart disease, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy or Kawasaki disease.
schema_org.name: ZZU pECG (Zhengzhou University Pediatric ECG Database)
